Surface corresponds to adsorbent: the surface of activated carbon can adsorb various impurities and harmful substances. The surface of the sponge absorbs liquid through the adsorbent. Both have adsorption functions.

background.source: Activated carbon, also known as activated charcoal, is a highly porous form of carbon that is widely used to filter impurities from liquids and gases. With its small, low-volume pores, activated carbon is capable of adsorbing molecules and chemical compounds from its surroundings, making it an effective filter for a variety of applications. In fact, one gram of activated carbon has a surface area in excess of 3,000 m2, allowing it to capture and remove even tiny particles and impurities. Activated carbon is often derived from waste products like coconut husks and paper mill waste, and can be further enhanced with chemical treatments to improve its adsorption properties. Whether you're looking to purify water, clean the air, or filter other liquids and gases, activated carbon is an effective and reliable solution for removing impurities at the molecular level.
background.target: Sponges are fascinating and unique creatures belonging to the phylum Porifera. As the sister group of all other animals, they are the first branch off the evolutionary tree from the last common ancestor. Sponges have bodies full of pores and channels that allow water to circulate through them and consist of jelly-like mesohyl sandwiched between two thin layers of cells. Their cells are unspecialized and can transform into other types, enabling them to migrate between the main cell layers and the mesohyl. Despite not having complex nervous, digestive, or circulatory systems, sponges have developed the ability to maintain a constant water flow through their bodies to obtain food and oxygen and to remove wastes. One unique quality of sponges is their adsorbent property, allowing them to filter pollutants and other particles from the water as it passes through their bodies.
